name: hh_mm_ss<_Duration>::hh_mm_ss(_Duration __d)
prose: Explicit constexpr noexcept constructor of hh_mm_ss. It initializes, in member order: __is_neg_ = (__d < _Duration(0)); __h_ = duration_cast<hours>(abs(__d)); __m_ = duration_cast<minutes>(abs(__d) - hours()); __s_ = duration_cast<seconds>(abs(__d) - hours() - minutes()); __f_ = duration_cast<precision>(abs(__d) - hours() - minutes() - seconds()), where precision is duration<common_type rep, ratio<1, 10^fractional_width>> and fractional_width is the number of decimal digits needed for the denominator of common_type_t<_Duration, seconds>::period when that denominator has a terminating decimal expansion of fewer than 19 digits, else 6. All four stored parts are non-negative (the sign is kept only in __is_neg_). duration_cast truncates toward zero, so the sub-second part keeps the exact remainder when the period's denominator divides a power of ten within the width limit, and drops the remainder below 10^-6 s otherwise (denominators with a non-terminating decimal expansion, such as 3). It acquires no resources.
note: Round-15 reviewer right: the width cap of 6 applies when the denominator has no terminating decimal expansion (__width reaches 19, hh_mm_ss.h:42-50), not whenever the denominator is not a power of ten; the original reviewer was right that truncation can lose value in that case.

name: condition_variable::wait_for(unique_lock<mutex>&, const duration<_Rep, _Period>&)
prose: Member function template returning cv_status. If __d <= __d.zero() it returns cv_status::timeout immediately without examining __lk or waiting. Otherwise it records steady_clock::now() as __c_now, computes the current time since epoch in nanoseconds with __safe_nanosecond_cast (of the steady clock when _LIBCPP_HAS_COND_CLOCKWAIT, otherwise of system_clock::now()) and __d in nanoseconds (a nonzero integer duration that rounds to 0 ns becomes 1 ns; out-of-range values saturate), and calls __do_timed_wait with the absolute time now + d, or with that clock's time_point::max() if the sum would overflow. It then returns cv_status::no_timeout if steady_clock::now() - __c_now < __d, else cv_status::timeout (so a spurious or early wakeup shorter than __d reports no_timeout). __do_timed_wait is noexcept, so if __lk does not own its mutex or the underlying wait fails with an error other than ETIMEDOUT, the exception from __throw_system_error ends in std::terminate rather than reaching the caller.
note: Reviewers (rounds 2, 15) right in effect: errors terminate through the noexcept __do_timed_wait and the early return skips the lock check; round 1 about the predicate belongs to the predicate overload. condition_variable.h:142-166.

name: condition_variable::wait_for(unique_lock<mutex>&, const duration<_Rep, _Period>&, _Predicate)
prose: Member function template returning bool, defined out of line: returns wait_until(__lk, steady_clock::now() + __d, std::move(__pred)). wait_until with a predicate loops: while __pred() is false it calls the time-point wait_until(__lk, __t); if that returns cv_status::timeout the function returns the value of one more __pred() call (so it can return true for a predicate that became true after the deadline) and otherwise keeps looping; if __pred() is true it returns true. If __pred() is true on entry it returns true without waiting and without checking __lk. The time-point wait_until returns timeout without waiting if the deadline has already passed, otherwise it calls the noexcept __do_timed_wait (which terminates the program if the mutex is not owned or the pthread wait fails other than by timeout). With __lk locked on entry, the predicate is evaluated with it locked and it is still locked on return.
note: Reviewers right: round 1 (predicate re-evaluated after timeout, already in the old prose), round 2 (noexcept leads to termination), round 15 (true-predicate and expired-deadline paths do not check the lock); condition_variable.h:131-139, 190-194.

name: condition_variable::__do_timed_wait(unique_lock<mutex>&, time_point<steady_clock, nanoseconds>)
prose: Private noexcept member, defined only when _LIBCPP_HAS_COND_CLOCKWAIT. If __lk does not own its mutex it calls std::__throw_system_error(EPERM, ...), which in a noexcept function ends in std::terminate. Otherwise it converts the time point's nanoseconds since epoch into a timespec: seconds via duration_cast, and if the seconds count is less than the maximum tv_sec it sets tv_sec and tv_nsec = the remainder, else tv_sec = maximum and tv_nsec = 999999999. It calls pthread_cond_clockwait(&__cv_, __lk.mutex()->native_handle(), CLOCK_MONOTONIC, &__ts); an ETIMEDOUT result is treated as a normal return, and any other nonzero result calls std::__throw_system_error (terminating). On a normal return the mutex has been re-acquired. It returns nothing.
note: Reviewers' points (noexcept termination, nonpositive duration skipping the lock check) concern wait_for, not this function: the old prose already said EPERM terminates; this function itself has no nonpositive-duration shortcut. condition_variable.h:197-217.

name: condition_variable::__do_timed_wait(unique_lock<mutex>&, time_point<_Clock, nanoseconds>) [generic template]
prose: Private noexcept member template: computes __tp - _Clock::now() and calls wait_for(__lk, thatDuration), discarding the cv_status result. wait_for returns immediately, without checking __lk, if the duration is not positive; otherwise the wait goes through the wait_for duration overload and its calls of the clock-specific __do_timed_wait overloads. Any exception from the nested calls (for a mutex not owned or a failed wait) leaves a noexcept function and ends in std::terminate. It returns nothing.
note: condition_variable.h:220-224; the lock-owns claim of the old prose is only an effect of a successful timed wait.
